**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER**

a) What **three** evidences exist to show that the world has warmed during the Quaternary period or since the late 19th Century?

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Quaternary** is the last 2.6 million years (the Ice Age period, with alternating cold glacial periods and warmer interglacials, and the present Holocene warm period of the last 11,700 years). Three lines of evidence are given (3 marks each); two cover the long-term warming since the last glacial period, and one covers the period since the late 19th century.

**1. Instrumental temperature records (since the late 19th century).** Thermometer records from weather stations, ships and buoys, and later satellites, show that the **global mean surface temperature has risen by about 1 degree Celsius (about 1.1) since the period 1850 to 1900**, with most of the rise since the 1970s; the last decade was the warmest on record and most of the warmest years have occurred in the last few decades. Warming of the oceans has also been measured.

**2. The shrinking of ice and the rise of sea level.** Most **mountain glaciers have retreated** (for example in the Alps, the Himalayas, the Andes, and the loss of most of the ice cap of Mount Kilimanjaro since the early 20th century), the **Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets** are losing mass, the area of **Arctic sea ice** has fallen, and permafrost is thawing. Meltwater and thermal expansion of the oceans have raised the **sea level by about 20 cm since 1900**. In the Quaternary, the retreat of ice from the last glacial maximum (about 20,000 years ago) is shown by **glacial landforms** (moraines, drumlins, striated rocks and U-shaped valleys) found far south of the present ice limits in Europe and North America.

**3. Proxy (indirect) evidence of past climate.** **Ice cores** from Greenland and Antarctica (the oxygen isotope ratios, and the trapped bubbles of air, showing temperature and carbon dioxide concentrations) show the glacial and interglacial cycles and the rise of temperature at the end of the last ice age and since; **deep-sea sediment cores** (the oxygen isotopes in microscopic shells of foraminifera); **pollen analysis** (the vegetation changes from tundra and cold-tolerant plants to forest in the warm periods); **tree rings** and **coral growth** show the rate of growth and temperature changes in recent centuries; and the **upward and poleward shift** of species and the earlier arrival of spring (phenology) are also evidence.

(Also acceptable: historical records such as the dates of grape harvests and of freezing of rivers, and increased frequency of heat waves.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) For each of the following environmental hazards, suggest **two** measures that could be taken to minimize their negative effects:

(i) Land pollution

(ii) Drought.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four measures are suggested (2 marks each: the measure and a short explanation).

**(i) Land pollution** (the contamination of soil and land by solid waste, plastics, chemicals, oil, mining and industrial waste)

1. **Proper waste management: reduce, reuse, recycle and safe disposal.** Provide waste collection and **sanitary landfills**, compost organic waste, recycle plastics, metal and glass, and treat hazardous industrial and medical waste before disposal, so that little rubbish is dumped on land. Many countries, Cameroon included, have laws that ban or restrict non-biodegradable plastic bags.
2. **Laws, control and clean-up (polluter pays).** Enforce environmental laws with inspections, **fines** and the obligation on firms to restore polluted sites; carry out **clean-up and rehabilitation** of the contaminated land (removal of waste, bioremediation by bacteria, phytoremediation by plants, and the replanting of mined land); and control the use of **fertilisers and pesticides** (organic farming, integrated pest management). Public education on littering supports these measures.

**(ii) Drought** (a long period of abnormally low rainfall, leading to water shortage and crop failure, as in the Sahel and the Far North of Cameroon)

1. **Water storage, supply and conservation.** Build **dams, reservoirs, boreholes, wells and rainwater-harvesting tanks**, transfer water by pipelines, and use water efficiently (**drip irrigation**, recycling, the repair of leaks) to store water in the wet season for use in the dry period.
2. **Drought-resistant farming and land management, with early warning and relief.** Introduce **drought-resistant and early-maturing crop varieties** (sorghum, millet, cassava), **mulching, soil conservation and tree planting** (shelter belts, the Great Green Wall initiative in the Sahel) to keep moisture, control the number of livestock, and diversify livelihoods; use **weather forecasting and early warning systems**, and keep food reserves and organise emergency relief and insurance.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Using examples of towns in Cameroon, consider any **three** major reasons responsible for the occurrence of urban floods.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Urban floods are common in many Cameroonian towns, for example **Douala, Yaounde, Limbe, Bamenda, Maroua and Garoua**, especially in the rainy season. Three major reasons are considered (about 2.5 marks each).

**1. Heavy and intense rainfall on low-lying or sloping land.** Douala and Limbe, on the Gulf of Guinea coast, have some of the highest rainfall in Africa (more than 3,000 mm a year in Douala, much of it falling in intense storms in July to September), and Douala lies on a low, flat, swampy site near the Wouri estuary, where the **water table is high** and the tide impedes the flow of the rivers to the sea. The water cannot run off or drain away quickly, so the streets and the low-lying districts are flooded. In Yaounde heavy storms cause floods in the valleys of the streams of the Mfoundi basin, and in Limbe the water rushes down the steep slopes of Mount Cameroon.

**2. Inadequate, blocked and poorly maintained drainage.** The drains and gutters are too small, were designed for a smaller population, or do not exist in the unplanned districts, and they are **blocked by solid waste (plastic bags, rubbish) and silt**, so that water backs up and overflows; this is a major cause of floods in Douala and Yaounde. Poor waste collection and the lack of maintenance make it worse.

**3. Building on flood plains, wetlands and river channels, and the increase of impermeable surfaces.** Rapid, **unplanned urban growth** has led people to build houses on swamps, stream banks and in valley bottoms (the marshes of Douala, the stream valleys of Yaounde), and the wetlands and mangroves that absorbed the floods have been filled in. The expansion of roofs, roads and pavements **reduces infiltration** and increases runoff, and the removal of vegetation on the hillsides increases the runoff; the streams narrow and the flood peaks are higher and faster.

(Other reason: the **release of water from dams**, for example from the Lagdo dam on the Benue, which has caused flooding in Garoua and downstream, and weak enforcement of the building regulations and the land-use plan.)

**Conclusion:** urban floods result from natural factors (heavy rain, low relief, a high water table), made much worse by human factors (poor drainage and waste management, and unplanned building on flood-prone land).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR**

a) Explain **THREE** measures that can be put in place to promote international and bilateral trade.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**International trade** is trade between countries in general, and **bilateral trade** is trade between two countries. Three measures that can promote it are explained (2 marks each).

**1. Reduction of trade barriers and trade agreements.** Governments can lower or remove **tariffs, quotas and non-tariff barriers** by negotiating within the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, by **bilateral agreements** between two countries (with preferential tariffs) and by **regional trading blocs** (CEMAC, ECOWAS, the European Union, the African Continental Free Trade Area, AfCFTA), and by the **Economic Partnership Agreement** with the European Union; this widens the market, lowers the price of goods and increases the flow of trade.

**2. Improvement of transport, communications and port infrastructure.** Good roads, railways, deep-sea ports, airports, storage facilities and telecommunications lower the cost and time of moving goods and so promote trade (for example the Kribi deep-sea port in Cameroon, and the road and rail corridors that link the port of Douala to Chad and the Central African Republic). Simple, fast **customs procedures** (one-stop border posts, electronic documents) work in the same way.

**3. Export promotion, incentives and macro-economic stability.** Governments and trade bodies can organise **trade fairs and missions**, give **export incentives** (tax relief, credit and insurance, and export-processing or free zones), improve the **quality and standards** of the products and diversify exports; a **stable currency** (such as the CFA franc, which is tied to the euro) and political peace and security also give confidence to traders.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Discuss **THREE** factors and **TWO** impacts of Globalisation.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Globalisation** is the growing integration and interdependence of the world's economies, societies and cultures through the movement of goods, services, capital, technology, information and people. The factors and impacts are discussed below (about 6 marks for the factors and 4 marks for the impacts).

**Three factors that have caused globalisation**

1. **Advances in transport technology.** Containerisation, larger ships, jet aircraft, and better roads and railways have **cut the time and cost** of moving goods and people, so that firms can produce in one country and sell in another.
2. **The information and communication technology revolution.** The Internet, mobile telephones, satellites and fibre-optic cables allow instant communication, international financial transactions, e-commerce and the management of a production system that is spread over many countries.
3. **Trade liberalisation and the role of transnational corporations (TNCs).** The reduction of tariffs and barriers (GATT and the WTO, and regional agreements), the deregulation of finance, the end of the Cold War and the opening of China, India and Eastern Europe, have encouraged **TNCs** to invest abroad (foreign direct investment) and to place production where labour and materials are cheapest, and have created global markets and brands.

**Two impacts of globalisation**

1. **Economic growth, investment and technology transfer (positive).** Globalisation has brought **foreign investment, jobs, technology and wider markets**, cheaper and more varied goods for consumers, and the rapid growth of countries such as China and the Asian newly industrialised countries, and has helped to reduce poverty in many places; the countries can specialise in what they do best.
2. **Widening inequalities, the loss of local industries and cultural and environmental damage (negative).** The gap between rich and poor countries and between rich and poor people within countries has **widened**: small local firms and farmers cannot compete with imported goods or with TNCs (for example the effect of cheap imports of second-hand clothes and frozen chicken on local producers in Africa), jobs are lost in the older industrial areas of the rich countries (deindustrialisation), workers may be paid low wages in poor conditions, the culture and languages become more uniform, resource use and pollution increase, and countries become **vulnerable to world economic crises** (such as the financial crisis of 2008) and to disease (COVID-19) that spread rapidly.

**Conclusion:** globalisation has benefited countries and people able to take part in it, but has created losers; its effects depend on the strength of the economy, and on government policy.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) What **THREE** strategies can Cameroon adopt to become a Newly Industrialised Country?

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **Newly Industrialised Country (NIC)** is a developing country whose economy has moved quickly from agriculture and the export of raw materials to manufacturing and services, with fast growth, rising incomes and a large share of manufactured exports (for example South Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia, Brazil and, later, China). Cameroon's long-term plan (**Vision 2035**) aims to make it an **emerging**, newly industrialised country. Three strategies are proposed (3 marks each).

**1. Add value to the raw materials by local processing, and promote manufacturing for export.** Cameroon exports mostly **raw or semi-processed products** (crude oil, timber, cocoa, coffee, cotton, bananas, rubber and minerals). It should process them locally (sawmilling and furniture, chocolate and cocoa products, textile and garment making from cotton, food processing, aluminium and metal products, refining and petrochemicals) and **export manufactured goods**, supported by industrial zones and **export-processing or free zones**, and an export-oriented policy and import substitution for local needs; this creates more jobs and earns more foreign exchange.

**2. Develop the infrastructure and energy supply.** Reliable and cheap **electricity** (dams such as Lom Pangar, Memve'ele and Nachtigal, gas and solar power), **roads, railways, deep-sea ports** (the Kribi port), airports, water supply and telecommunications are needed for industry; these reduce production costs and link the factories with the markets and ports. Public-private partnerships and loans can finance them.

**3. Improve human capital, investment, governance and markets.** Invest in **technical and vocational education, science and research**, so that workers have the skills for industry and technology can be adapted; create a **good business climate** (stable and transparent laws, less corruption, tax incentives, easy credit for small and medium enterprises, protection of property) to attract **foreign direct investment** and local capital; and use the larger markets of **CEMAC and the African Continental Free Trade Area** for the sale of goods, with trade agreements with the rest of the world.

(Other strategies: agricultural modernisation to supply industry, diversification of the economy, the promotion of tourism and services, and a stable macro-economic policy.)
